title: Web Document History and the Evolution of HTML Standards
learningObjectives: Describe the early purpose of HTML as a markup format for linked documents on the Web.
Explain why shared HTML specifications were needed as browsers and web publishing grew.
Identify major historical HTML milestones including HTML 2.0, HTML 3.2, HTML 4.01 and HTML5.
Distinguish a published standards milestone from a browser implementation or vendor-specific extension.
Explain the significance of the W3C HTML5 Recommendation in 2014 without treating it as the end of HTML development.
Describe the role of WHATWG and the HTML Living Standard in ongoing HTML development.
Explain how standards improve interoperability across browsers, devices and assistive technologies.
Recognize that older HTML versions remain historically important but modern authors should follow current standards and compatibility guidance.
Use standards documentation and browser support information to verify an HTML feature before relying on it.
Summarize HTML evolution as a progression toward richer semantics, native media, application capabilities and more consistent browser behaviour.

understand.concept: HTML began as a way to structure linked documents for the early Web. As more browsers and publishers adopted it, shared specifications became important so the same document could be interpreted consistently. HTML evolved through several published specifications and implementation eras. Modern HTML is not a completely separate language called HTML5 that stopped changing; it is maintained as a living standard with ongoing refinements.
understand.whyItMatters: History explains why HTML emphasizes document structure, semantics and interoperability. It also helps developers distinguish standard features from old browser-specific workarounds and avoid learning obsolete markup as current practice.
understand.history: A reliable high-level timeline is: HTML 2.0 was published as an IETF standard in 1995; HTML 3.2 became a W3C Recommendation in 1997; HTML 4.01 followed in 1999; HTML5 became a W3C Recommendation in 2014; and the WHATWG HTML Living Standard continues to evolve. These milestones describe specifications and publication events, not the exact date every browser implemented each feature.
understand.analogy: HTML standards are like shared rules for writing documents that many different readers and tools must understand. As needs changed, the rules were extended while compatibility with existing documents remained important.
understand.analogyLimit: Standards development is not a simple sequence in which every browser switches versions on one date. Specifications, browser implementations, testing and real-world adoption overlap. A recommendation or living standard does not guarantee identical support for every feature in every browser.

explain.narrative:
The Web needed a common way to describe linked documents. HTML supplied elements for headings, paragraphs, links and other content structures. As the Web expanded, browser vendors and authors needed shared rules so a document would not require a different version for each browser.

HTML 2.0 was published as an IETF standard in 1995. HTML 3.2 became a W3C Recommendation in 1997, followed by HTML 4.01 in 1999. These specifications helped consolidate common practice and document features used by browsers. Later, work on HTML5 addressed the needs of a Web that had become more application-oriented, including native audio and video, canvas and richer semantic and form features. W3C published HTML5 as a Recommendation in 2014.

The history did not stop there. The WHATWG continues work on the HTML Living Standard, which is updated as the platform evolves. Browser vendors implement features over time, and interoperability depends on tests and real implementation behaviour as well as specification text. This is why modern developers should consult current documentation and compatibility information rather than memorizing version labels as if they were separate languages.

When researching an HTML feature, ask three questions: what does the current standard specify, which browsers support it, and what fallback is needed for the users and environments the project serves? Historical knowledge is useful when reading old code, but new projects should use current semantic markup and avoid obsolete presentational elements.

examples.code:
My website

Modern HTML gives content meaningful structure.
examples.explanation: This example uses header and main elements to give page regions meaningful structure. HTML has evolved through standards and browser implementations; modern HTML is maintained as a living standard.
examples.expectedOutput: The browser displays the meaningful HTML content.

examples.title: A simplified HTML standards timeline
examples.code:
1995  HTML 2.0 — IETF standard
1997  HTML 3.2 — W3C Recommendation
1999  HTML 4.01 — W3C Recommendation
2014  HTML5 — W3C Recommendation
Today WHATWG HTML Living Standard — ongoing evolution
examples.explanation: The timeline records selected specification milestones. It does not imply that browsers implemented every feature on those dates or that the current Web is frozen at HTML5.
examples.expectedOutput: You can place the major milestones in order and explain why standards continued to evolve.

examples.title: Verify a feature before using it
examples.code:
Feature: <dialog>
1. Read the current HTML standard or MDN reference.
2. Check browser support for target environments.
3. Test keyboard and assistive-technology behaviour.
4. Add a fallback if required by the support policy.
5. Record the decision in project documentation.
examples.explanation: A historical milestone does not tell you whether a feature is safe to use in every current browser. Check the current specification, support data and the actual user requirements.
examples.expectedOutput: A documented decision based on standards and compatibility evidence.

examples.title: Specification and browser implementation are related but distinct
examples.code:
HTML standard → defines parsing and element behaviour
Browser engine → implements the specification
Web platform tests → check interoperable behaviour
Website → uses features supported by its target browsers
examples.explanation: A specification describes expected behaviour. Browser engines implement it, and tests help detect differences. A standards document alone is not proof that every browser has shipped a feature.
examples.expectedOutput: You can distinguish a standard, an implementation and a compatibility test.

practise.guidedTask: Create a short timeline with the four major milestones in the lesson. For each one, record the organization and what changed. Then choose one modern HTML element and verify its current specification, browser support and accessibility behaviour.
practise.independentTask: Write a standards-aware feature note for a modern HTML element. Include its semantic purpose, relevant standard documentation, browser support, accessibility considerations and a fallback decision. Explain why a version label alone is not enough to decide whether the feature can be used.
hints: A standards milestone is not the same as the day a browser shipped a feature.
HTML 2.0 was an IETF standard; later milestones were W3C Recommendations.
HTML5 became a W3C Recommendation in 2014, but HTML development continued.
The WHATWG HTML Living Standard is maintained on an ongoing basis.
Use current standards and browser support data when building new projects.

questions.prompt: What is HTML primarily responsible for?
questions.explanation: HTML describes document structure and meaning.

questions.prompt: How does a browser use HTML?
options: Parses document structure and builds a DOM
Always treats it only as an image
questions.answer: Parses document structure and builds a DOM
questions.explanation: The DOM represents document nodes and their relationships.

questions.prompt: Which organization published HTML5 as a W3C Recommendation in 2014?
questions.explanation: W3C published HTML5 as a Recommendation in 2014. This was a standards milestone, not the end of HTML evolution.

questions.prompt: What best describes the current HTML Living Standard?
options: An ongoing standard that continues to evolve
A browser-specific extension that never changes
A replacement for all CSS specifications
questions.answer: An ongoing standard that continues to evolve
questions.explanation: The WHATWG HTML Living Standard is maintained as an evolving specification.

questions.prompt: Why should developers check browser support in addition to reading a specification?
options: Browser implementations may ship features at different times or have compatibility differences.
A specification is only a colour palette.
Browser support determines the HTML file extension.
questions.answer: Browser implementations may ship features at different times or have compatibility differences.
questions.explanation: Specifications define intended behaviour; browser implementations and compatibility data show what users can actually rely on.
